newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Asian Development Bank to double loans to Kazakhs.
newsitem.headline: Asian Development Bank to double loans to Kazakhs.

text.p: The Asian Development Bank, which has granted Kazakhstan a total of $230 million, plans to double this figure by the year 2000, seeking closer cooperation with the resource-rich country, the bank's mission said on Tuesday.

"In the first three years with the bank, the loans have totalled about $230 million, and we expect to double that roughly over the next three years," Peter Sullivan, Region East Vice-President, told a news conference.
Sullivan said the bank had initially planned to invest this year a total of $85 million in Kazakhstan's water resources management and land improvement programmes and education.
But he said that the Kazakh government had asked the bank to grant an additional $100 million to support reform of the national pension scheme.

"Assuming that things went smoothly, we hope to be able to process this project by about November this year," Sullivan said. He added the pension programme loan could be granted at around seven percent annual interest with a grace period of two years.

Kazakhstan's government, facing a huge backlog of unpaid pensions worth $500 million and admitting that the state-run pension fund has gone bankrupt, plans to set the pension reform in motion in January 1998.

The reform, whose draft has already been submitted to law-makers for approval and is currently undergoing a nationwide discussion, is aimed at creating a network of private pension funds, alongside an improved state-run one, and a number of financial companies which will manage their assets.
The reform, which targets making pension funds influential players on Kazakhstan's markets of government securities and equities, is being completed over 30 years.
Oil-rich Kazakhstan -- five times the size of France -- has so far attracted around $3.5 billion of direct foreign investment, with investment commitments totalling another $50 billion.
Sullivan held out the prospect that in time, the Central Asian state could become one of the bank's wealthiest members.
"We are looking forward for a day, not many years from now, when oil and gas and infrastructure are developed, and we hope that some day Kazakhstan will be a donor rather than a borrower," he said.
